clue.text: Way to get round minor predicament

parts.note: by- as a prefix means minor or secondary, as in a by-road or by-election
a pass is a predicament, as in 'things have come to a pretty pass'

explanation.surface: A small spot of bother that needs some clever route around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A road that skirts a town is a route for avoiding the centre, i.e. a way round.

clue.text: Stigma on flower being the wrong way up? That takes the biscuit!

parts.note: a brand is a mark of disgrace, a stigma

indicators.note: in a down entry, a word placed the wrong way up is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a pansy is a garden flower

explanation.surface: A botanist notices a flower's stigma sits upside down and finds it the last straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being the wrong way up' turns PANSY into YSNAP. 'Stigma' looks botanical, but it is the brand of disgrace. 'That takes the biscuit!' also plays on the idiom for something outrageous.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp rolled ginger wafer, often cream-filled, is a classic British teatime biscuit.

clue.text: How to calculate the probability of one of Jesus' miracles entailing pain, as Sade would see it

definitions.text: one of Jesus' miracles entailing pain, as Sade would see it

explanation.surface: A mathematician sizes up the odds of a Gospel miracle through the eyes of a notorious French marquis.
explanation.walkthrough: In French, poisson is fish and pain is bread, so the feeding of the five thousand, sharing out loaves and fishes, becomes a 'fish distribution' to a Frenchman like the Marquis de Sade.
explanation.definitionFit: A statistical model giving the chance of a number of events in a fixed interval; also, in French, the sharing out of fish that went with the bread.

clue.text: Take a good, hard look, we hear, at what the steps may involve

indicators.note: signals that the phrase before it is to be spoken and matched by sound

parts.note: to stare well is to take a good, hard look

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to examine carefully what climbing some steps would entail.
explanation.definitionFit: The vertical shaft in a building that a staircase climbs through is where the steps are found.

clue.text: Bigamy is incomprehensible

explanation.surface: Someone declares that having two spouses at once makes no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney slang 'my old Dutch' is a wife (from 'Duchess of Fife'), so having two of them is a cheeky reading of bigamy.
explanation.definitionFit: Two wives in slang terms; also gibberish, a phrase for talk nobody can follow.

clue.text: Public required too much — junk axed

indicators.note: to junk something is to throw it away, so the following word is dropped from the longer one

parts.note: to overtax is to demand too much of someone, so required too much is overtaxed
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: The public were asked for too much, so the rubbish was cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in public view is open and unconcealed.

clue.text: Remained without curve and lines of identification

indicators.note: an old sense of without is outside, so the first word's letters go round the second's

parts.note: bode is an old past tense of bide, to remain
an arc is a curve

explanation.surface: Something stayed straight and was marked by lines that identify it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here is the old sense of outside, not lacking; 'Remained' looks like it wants a modern synonym, but the archaic past tense of bide is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: The printed stripes scanned at a till identify a product, so they are lines used for identification.

clue.text: Tied loosely for 1 4 change

indicators.note: something tied loosely can be rearranged, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

explanation.surface: A knot done up loosely needs altering.
explanation.walkthrough: The '1 4' appears to be a cross-reference to 1-across and 4-across and plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise or amend a text is to alter it.

clue.text: Not derived from cad and liar acting together

indicators.note: two words working together are combined and their letters shuffled as one pool

explanation.surface: A rogue and a fibber team up in some shady scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or quantity at the root is basic, not derived from anything else, as with a radical in language or chemistry.

clue.text: Exercise forbearance, encountering burden

explanation.surface: Someone shows restraint when faced with a heavy load.
explanation.walkthrough: 'burden' here is the old sense of a song's chorus, not a load.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold back or abstain from acting; also the repeated chorus of a song, once called its burden.

clue.text: Reverse location of

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Reverse location of', cut short with no enumeration; a search of the exact text found nothing more.

clue.text: See 2
Smash attic to pieces — they gasp!

indicators.note: smashing something to pieces breaks it up, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks the loft, and onlookers gasp at the destruction.
explanation.definitionFit: People with a chronic breathing condition often struggle for air and wheeze.

clue.text: Meaning might be touching

explanation.surface: A remark's significance could be quite moving.
explanation.walkthrough: Touch is one of the five faculties of perception, so 'touching' could be one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The import of a word; also any faculty of perception, of which touch is one.

clue.text: System is what's central to runic poetry

indicators.note: the central part of a word is everything but its first and last letters

parts.note: verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Someone claims a whole system lies at the heart of ancient runic poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: The cosmos is everything, an all-embracing system of stars and galaxies.

clue.text: Ask Nina — I'd nitpick, holding up potential means of redaction

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the held letters are read bottom to top
the run of words holds the answer's letters inside them

explanation.surface: A fussy person offers to go over Nina's work and blot out the bad bits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding up' does two things: 'holding' signals letters held in 'Ask Nina — I'd nitpick', and 'up' reads them backwards, KNINAIDNI turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Black drawing ink could be used to blot out sensitive text before a document is released.

clue.text: Barenboim's left hand plays scales loudly, using this

definitions.text: Barenboim's left hand plays scales loudly, using this

indicators.note: the left-hand end of a written word is its first letter
playing about with letters means rearranging them

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: The pianist Daniel Barenboim practises scales forte with his left hand, reading a particular stave.
explanation.walkthrough: The left hand of a pianist usually reads music on the lower stave, marked with this symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: The F symbol on the lower stave fixes low notes, the ones a pianist's left hand usually plays.

clue.text: Help one reportedly popping up every 60 seconds

indicators.note: signals that the word meant is to be heard, not seen

parts.note: from the saying 'there's a sucker born every minute', a dupe appears every sixty seconds

explanation.surface: A helper apparently turns up once a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'there's a sucker born every minute' gives the gullible one.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid or relief given in time of need is assistance.

clue.text: See 4
Sexually harass rival at university

parts.note: to touch someone is to rival them, as in 'nobody can touch her'
being up means in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A competitor at college behaves inappropriately.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb for groping someone, i.e. making unwanted physical advances.

clue.text: Short note I put between accounts, aiming to undermine receiver's assessment from the beginning

indicators.note: one piece is placed between two others, so it sits inside the pair

parts.note: acc is short for account, and the plural gives two of them
aiming at, so aiming gives at

indicators.note: the first letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: A brief memo slipped among financial records aims to cast doubt on the official receiver's report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from the beginning' takes U, R and A, the opening letters of 'undermine receiver's assessment'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grace note crushed against the main note, sounded as briefly as possible, is a very short ornament in music.

clue.text: No-brainer to be content and sluggish

indicators.note: the answer is the content of the words, held inside them

explanation.surface: Someone says it is obvious to settle down and be idle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' means satisfied in the surface but contents for the solver: the letters sit inside 'brainer to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking the power to move, inactive and slow, is lethargic.

clue.text: Support for head of police

parts.note: pro means for or in favour of

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Backing given to the chief constable.
explanation.definitionFit: A post or beam holding something up is a supporting piece.

clue.text: Are poor tariffs providing return for soldier?

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards
the words supply the letters from within themselves

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether low import duties will pay off for a serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'providing return' means the words 'Are poor tariffs' supply the letters REPOORT, which read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavalry or armoured private is a mounted fighting man.

clue.text: Something worn in bed that's nearly formal dress

parts.note: nigh means nearly, almost
a tie is a standard part of formal dress, as in a dress code of black tie

explanation.surface: Bedwear that almost counts as evening attire.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose gown for sleeping in is nightwear.

clue.text: Produce copy at constant speed

parts.note: pi is the mathematical constant relating a circle's circumference to its diameter
rate means speed

explanation.surface: A printing press runs off copies at a steady pace.
explanation.definitionFit: To reproduce material illegally, such as films or software, is to make unauthorised copies.

clue.text: Retiring type is keeping a thousand animals

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: an OAP, old-age pensioner, is someone who has retired
K is the abbreviation for a thousand
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy person keeps a thousand creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' suggests shyness or a reversal, but here it means having retired: a pensioner. OAP is the British abbreviation for an old-age pensioner.
explanation.definitionFit: Giraffe relatives from the Congo with striped legs are African mammals.
